segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I saw an angel coming down from heaven, holding the key to the abyss and a great chain in his hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the Devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and threw him into the abyss, and shut and sealed it over him, so that he would no longer lead the nations astray until the thousand years were completed. After that he must be released for a short time.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I saw thrones, and they sat on them, and judgment was given to them. And I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded because of the testimony of Jesus and because of the word of God, and those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received the mark on their forehead or on their hand. They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were completed. This is the first resurrection.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection! Over these the second death has no authority, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when the thousand years are completed, Satan will be released from his prison,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he will go out to lead astray the nations at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for the war; their number is like the sand of the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the holy ones and the beloved city. And fire came down from heaven and consumed them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the devil, who was leading them astray, was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet also are, and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I saw a great white throne and the one seated on it. From his presence earth and heaven fled, and no place was found for them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw the dead, the great and the small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. And another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged from what was written in the books, according to their works.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The sea gave up the dead that were in it, and Death and Hades gave up the dead that were in them, and they were judged, each one according to their works.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And anyone not found written in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire.

notes.note: The KJV and several modern versions render this 'bottomless pit'. In the Septuagint the word means the primeval deep, and in Jewish writings of the period it had become a name for the underworld prison of rebellious spirits. 'Abyss' keeps that association without adding the image of a pit, which the Greek word does not itself supply.

This is the only passage in the New Testament that speaks of a thousand-year reign. Interpreters have long disagreed over whether it is a future period on earth after Christ's return, a symbolic picture of the present age between his resurrection and return, or something else. The translation does not decide between these readings.

Most translations have 'deceive'. The verb means to cause to wander or go off course, and in the Septuagint it is the usual word for leading people away into idolatry. 'Lead astray' keeps that sense of being drawn off the right path and not simply told something false.

The Greek word here is the same one translated 'Gentiles' elsewhere in the New Testament. It means peoples or nations, and in the plural often the non-Jewish peoples specifically. In Revelation the scope is the peoples of the whole world, so 'nations' is used.

The Greek can mean either that those seated were given authority to judge or that a verdict was given in their favor. The scene echoes Daniel 7:22, where the wording is similarly open. The text does not say who is seated on the thrones; the rendering leaves both questions as the Greek leaves them.

The verb is a simple past of 'live', which can mean 'they lived' or 'they came to life'. Most modern translations take it as 'came to life', as the same form is used of Christ's resurrection in 2:8. Whether this is a bodily resurrection or a spiritual one is disputed and is tied to how the thousand years are understood.

Most translations say the second death has no 'power' over them. The Greek word denotes the right or jurisdiction to act, not raw force, so 'authority' is the closer equivalent: the second death has no claim on these people.

The names come from Ezekiel 38–39, where Gog, of the land of Magog, leads a vast army against a restored Israel and is destroyed by God. By the first century the pair had become a byword in Jewish tradition for the hostile nations of the final battle. Here they stand for the nations of the whole earth, not for one identifiable people.

The traditional rendering is 'saints', which now suggests canonized individuals or people of unusual virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of God's people as those set apart for him, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

Many later manuscripts read 'from God out of heaven', and the KJV follows them. The shorter reading translated here has early support and is adopted by most modern critical editions. The longer form was probably influenced by the similar wording in 21:2 and 21:10.

A first-century reader would have pictured scrolls, not bound volumes. The image of heavenly records opened at the judgment comes from Daniel 7:10. The 'book of life' recalls a city's register of citizens, an image already used in the Old Testament (Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1).

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels, letters and Revelation, and translators divide between 'deceive', 'mislead' and 'lead astray', which readers would take as different words.
Very frequent across the New Testament and routinely split between 'power', 'authority' and 'right', which blurs its distinction from δύναμις.
Revelation uses it both for the sealed scroll of chapter 5 and the 'book of life'; a single policy on 'scroll' versus 'book' is needed across chapters, including for βίβλος.

candidates.reason: The 'ages of the ages' formula and related αἰών phrases recur throughout the New Testament and need one decision between idiomatic 'forever' and the literal 'ages'.
Ranges over 'life', 'self', 'person' and 'soul' across the New Testament, and the traditional 'soul' often imports a later body–soul dualism; it needs a sense-by-sense policy.
